video_title: 40 Years of Trading Lessons with Patrick Welton | Top Traders Unplugged | Ep.153
gist: Physician-turned-CTA founder Pat Welton (Welton Investment Corporation) recounts lessons from Paul Tudor Jones and John Henry, argues managing outside money is a moral duty that drove early-2000s vol targeting, decomposes trend returns into economic carry, financial carry, information diffusion and reflexivity, and rebuts claims that CTA industry capacity or multistrat pod shops impair trend following.

themes.theme: Market structure and lessons from Commodities Corp era

insights.claim: Paul Tudor Jones told Welton that once you trade size you cannot exit when you want, only when the market lets you, which taught Welton that markets are not math but a counterparty game.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Liquidity and exit capacity, not signal quality, constrain large traders.
insights.quote: when you start trading size, you can't only think about getting out when you want. you have to get out when the market lets you

insights.claim: Every trade has a counterparty who at that moment also believes they have an edge, so market structure matters in every aspect of trading.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Edge must be framed relative to who is on the other side.
insights.quote: there's somebody on the other side of every single trade who at that moment believes they also have an edge

insights.claim: Commodities Corporation in the late 1980s can reasonably be considered the first multi-strategy pod shop, and it also explicitly developed trading talent through senior-junior mentoring.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Today's pod-shop model has a decades-old template built on talent development.
insights.quote: Commodities Corporation, I think could could reasonably be thought of as the very first multistrategy pod shop of traders

insights.claim: Welton was allocated more capital every quarter at Commodities Corp as they hit return targets, a performance-gated capital model.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Illustrates early incremental, target-based allocation to traders.
insights.quote: we were allocated more money every quarter as we hit return targets

insights.claim: From visiting Tudor's growing firm ('manuals for all the manuals'), Welton concluded trading is only one component of building a professional trading firm.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Operational scaling is a distinct skill from trading.
insights.quote: trading was only one one component of building a professional trading firm

insights.claim: John Henry told Welton the difference between his success and others' was that they actually followed their system, and that the system could be printed on a billboard on Highway 101 because no one else would follow it.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Discipline and ownership of a system, not secrecy, is the durable edge.
insights.quote: the difference between our success and other people's is that we actually follow our system

insights.claim: Traders cannot exploit a borrowed system because they lack confidence in it; trader and methodology must be paired with conviction or the edge cannot be exploited through rough or calm periods.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Allocators should test manager conviction in their own process.
insights.quote: they have to pair themselves with a degree of confidence or there's really no way to exploit that edge through time

themes.theme: Managing outside money: moral duty and vol targeting

insights.claim: The real difference between prop trading and asset management is moral, not operational: once you take outside money, the client's goals become the number one goal and shape how risk is managed.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Product design should start from client goals, not trader's preferred risk metric.
insights.quote: the day you take somebody's outside money is the day you you make their goals the number one goal

insights.claim: Prop traders tend to optimize risk-adjusted return on capital (RAROC) and think in dollars, while managers of outside money must think in percentages and client-specific risk profiles.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Explains different sizing behaviour between prop and fiduciary trading.
insights.quote: most prop traders for themselves are probably thinking something on the order of a ray rock

insights.claim: Allocator-type clients want constant, targeted volatility, whereas investor-type clients may want more exposure when forward returns are better and less when weaker.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Two client archetypes require different risk regimes from the same strategy.
insights.quote: if they were more of an investor, they might want more exposure when there's a better value or when there's a better forward return profile

insights.claim: Welton's 1990s diversified medium-term trend program ran unfixed volatility averaging about 15 vol, ranging roughly 10 in low-opportunity to 20 in high-opportunity periods.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Pre-vol-targeting CTA track records embed much more variable risk.
insights.quote: its average volatility would be in in well approximately probably about a 15v in the '9s but that might be 10 v when there's less opportunity and 20 when there's more

insights.claim: In the early 2000s allocators complained they lost money three or four times faster than they made it with CTAs; Welton verified this was true because rising volatility and correlation increased net exposure, making reversals 3-4x faster in equity P&L.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Unmanaged vol/correlation expansion creates asymmetric drawdown speed.
insights.quote: a reversal in some cases was approximately three or four times faster in equity P&L

insights.claim: Beginning in the early 2000s many CTAs, including Welton, adopted volatility targeting of the portfolio or segments to mute these reversals and make CTAs compatible with professional allocators, which is why such asymmetry is not seen in track records today.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Comparing pre- and post-2000s CTA records requires adjusting for vol-targeting adoption.
insights.quote: in the early 2000s, many people including ourselves began volatility targeting the portfolio or volatility targeting segments of the portfolio

insights.claim: Some savvy investors were such good contrarian timers that when they doubled their account Welton was almost certain an industry drawdown was ending, and when they halved it the party was over.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Sophisticated flow into CTAs at drawdown troughs can be a contrarian signal.
insights.quote: when they would call and double the size of their account. I was almost certain that that was the end of any industry draw down

insights.claim: The usual tragedy of managed money is investors waiting for confirmation, getting in too late and putting themselves off-cycle; this return gap from switching on performance is usually the biggest cost investors face.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Holding discipline matters more than manager selection for realized returns.
insights.quote: the negative investor alpha that occurs from people switching on performance is is usually the biggest cost that they face

insights.claim: Welton says the biggest input to compounding is steady-handedness, i.e. how much your hand shakes.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Behavioral consistency is the core compounding driver.
insights.quote: steady-handedness compounds well

themes.theme: Edge, the four S's, and resisting marketing drift

insights.claim: One of the most damaging things traders do is change their strategy in response to marketing feedback to grow assets, a pattern seen across trend followers, hedge funds and private equity.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Style drift driven by client feedback erodes edge and results.
insights.quote: one of the most pernitious and damaging things I think traders have done to themselves is to respond to marketing feedback

insights.claim: Thirty to forty years ago manager interviews centered on four questions: what is your edge, how and where you exploit it, what is your risk management/position sizing, and how do you protect your tails.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: A compact due-diligence checklist versus modern 20-page pitch decks.
insights.quote: what's your edge in the marketplace? How and where are you going to exploit that edge? What is your risk management or position sizing?

insights.claim: There is reflexivity in the managed-money business: managers conform to what they think clients need, and clients then change what they want based on how managers evolved, so the true north must always be the market edge.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Results deteriorate as products drift from their underlying edge.
insights.quote: Is there a market edge? because if it starts to drift from that edge, results are just going to get worse

insights.claim: Pure trend following's edge comes from agnosticism and multi-asset, multidirectional participation, harvesting returns as capital moves between asset classes, sub-groups, long/short/flat over months and quarters, which delivers convexity and skew.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Constraining trend followers to fewer markets or long-only bias undermines the edge.
insights.quote: a pure trend follower has a very specific edge from agnosticism

insights.claim: Welton's 'four S's' framework for building a trading system: Setup (conditions raising Bayesian probability), Signal (entry/exit), Sizing (risk management including forward opportunity), and Symmetry (whether the trade has an asymmetric win/loss advantage).
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: A checklist for systematic or discretionary system design.
insights.quote: what is the setup for your trades?

insights.claim: Explaining the mechanics (daily math, formulas) rarely produces compelling investor-manager matches because it is facts without reason; such explanations are usually unappreciated or quickly forgotten.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: CTA marketing should explain return sources, not mechanics.
insights.quote: I think for the most part they're either unappreciated uh unmoved or quickly forgotten

themes.theme: Decomposing trend returns: carry, diffusion, reflexivity

insights.claim: Welton defines trend following as holding positions through time for a profit while buying strength and selling weakness, not predicting.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Definition centers time-held exposure rather than direction.
insights.quote: holding positions through time for a profit

insights.claim: Trend following returns can be decomposed into four components: economic trend/carry, financial carry, information diffusion, and reflexivity (Soros-style feedback loops where buying begets buying), each with different power and clocks by sector.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Return attribution makes trend's zero correlation and convexity intelligible to allocators.
insights.quote: one can decompose returns into the components of economic trend into financial carry into information diffusion and then into some form of reflexivity

insights.claim: Equity indices have strongly positive economic carry but faced negative financial carry most of the time and still came out ahead.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Carry components can offset; trend captures the net agnostically.
insights.quote: have a positive positive economic carry, for instance, in equity indices, which is extremely strong, but have faced for most of the time a negative financial carry and still come out of head

insights.claim: In fixed income futures, careful decomposition shows the majority, sometimes the vast majority, of trend returns are accumulated term structure (roll) premia.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Bond trend returns depend heavily on curve shape, so ZIRP/flat curves hurt.
insights.quote: the majority and in some cases the vast majority of returns will be accumulated term structure premia

insights.claim: In 2013 consensus expected interest rates to rise, yet in 2014 rates fell all year and trend followers made 20-30% while most forecasters were wrong; Welton sees a similar setup today.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Consensus rate forecasts are unreliable; agnostic trend can profit when they fail.
insights.quote: in 2014 interest rates went down the entire year and trend followers made 20 or 30%

insights.claim: Showing allocators plain return attributions they can derive independently of the trader's opinion makes them understand trend's zero correlation and positive convexity.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Attribution-led narrative is the most effective way to sell trend following.
insights.quote: They get why the correlation is zero. They get why it's positively convex

insights.claim: Short-term trading largely removes carry from returns (carry needs time), relying more on information diffusion, reflexivity, and flow effects such as rebalancing flows that matter most below ~10-day holding periods.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Short-term trend is a structurally different return source from long-term trend.
insights.quote: If I'm swimming for 20 hours, if I'm swimming for 3 seconds, the carry doesn't matter very much

insights.claim: Traditional trend-following approaches rarely make money at 3-5 day holding periods except in very large, high dollar-volatility contracts; even academic short-term trend studies average closer to one-month holds.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Very short-term trend is mostly a mirage; other techniques work better there.
insights.quote: there have been very few instances except for very large contracts, large dollar volatility of the contracts

insights.claim: ZIRP environments and narrow G7 rate spreads materially impair trend following because they shrink the financial carry trend followers harvest.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Wider rate differentials and steeper curves are a tailwind for CTAs.
insights.quote: It's definitely affected when spreads from in G7 environments all become extremely narrow

insights.claim: Welton runs fully separated strategies: trend uses only price; systematic macro uses only cross-asset, fundamental, government report and alternative data; short-term models focus on flows with holds well under 10 days.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Strict input separation maximizes diversification across sleeves.
insights.quote: Trend uses price. The macro trading uses only cross asset signals, fundamental signals, government reports, alternative data

insights.claim: Welton adds relative value baskets that are dollar-neutral (FX), rate-neutral (DV01) or commodity-neutral so they diversify without stacking on the main portfolio's thematic risks.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Neutralized RV sleeves add uncorrelated return to directional books.
insights.quote: you can build say a dollarneutral currency basket now you're not stacking on top of your dollar risk

insights.claim: A fifth Welton sleeve is a dedicated risk-off strategy that sells equities only when flow data show a rapid rise in hedging and mispricing activity, because others paying to neutralize risk raises Welton's edge.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Hedging-flow signals can time crisis alpha more precisely than trend alone.
insights.quote: a dedicated risk off sleeve which is only designed to sell equities when there's a rapid rise in flow data

insights.claim: Welton has traded vol arb, a stat arb program with thousands of trades per day, and trend following, and now focuses only on futures and foreign exchange.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Context for breadth of firm's research experience.
insights.quote: we now only focus on futures and foreign exchange

insights.claim: Welton separates replication as a valid mathematical technique (trend following itself replicates others via smoothed price signals) from productized replication sold via a 'hero's journey' narrative against expensive, opaque managers.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Judge replication products on mechanics and cost, not narrative.
insights.quote: I would separate replication from the mechanism of replicating and versus the productizing of replication

insights.claim: Welton replicated the trend replicators and got better performance via better smoothing and less rebalance churn; holding ETF market sets constant would not have changed results much.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Institutions can build their own replication cheaper than retail ETFs.
insights.quote: if we do replicate the replicators we actually end up with better performance

insights.claim: A $500 million institution need not use a retail replication product; it could implement the same idea fully funded with lower fees and better cash management.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Large allocators should consider in-house or separately managed replication.
insights.quote: if an institution wants to do $500 million they don't necessarily have to go into a retail product

insights.claim: Replication products appeal because they solve two allocator failure points: overall cost and manager selection risk.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Explains replication ETF demand despite weaker economics in active versions.
insights.quote: the overall cost or the manager selection risk those are those are two failure points

insights.claim: The claim that trend following has a capacity problem is wrong at the industry level: owning $200bn of the $250bn industry via an un-consolidated rollup of CTAs would produce identical performance, since aggregate diversification of approaches compensates for size.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Industry AUM growth is not by itself a threat to trend returns.
insights.quote: This whole narrative that a trend follower can get too big and somehow their returns will go away. No, not if they compensate

insights.claim: Individual managers have demonstrably overstepped capacity, less so in long-term trend; fixing it via diversifying methods risks looking like style drift, requiring years of trusted client dialogue.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Fast-asset-raising managers are most at risk of capacity-driven decay.
insights.quote: there are managers that have overstepped their capacity um less so I think in long-term trend following

insights.claim: Capacity problems show up first as objectively measured, upward-trending execution costs in a few less liquid markets (e.g. tin versus copper) before appearing across the book.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Monitor slippage by market as an early capacity warning.
insights.quote: they begin to see their execution costs rise objectively measured um and trend in a particular upward direction, they may have a capacity problem

insights.claim: Large multistrat pod funds have not made trend following harder; their high-leverage short-term arbitrage operates in different market surfaces and may even supply liquidity to trend followers.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Pod-shop growth is not a structural headwind for CTAs.
insights.quote: for most trend followers it's either not seen or it may even be providing a liquidity pool

insights.claim: Global investors, out of roughly $100 trillion in allocatable capital, are massively under-allocated to alternatives.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Long runway for alternatives and multistrat products.
insights.quote: massively underallocated to alternatives not over

insights.claim: Pension plans discovering via Monte Carlo that a two-sigma move could dump a $400m liability on a company earning $60m need trend following as a strategic tail hedge, a reality that Bill Sharpe's 'own everything' view does not address.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Tail-risk sensitivity, not return maximization, drives CTA demand.
insights.quote: a two sigma move on their pension plan, you know, might throw a $400 million liability onto a company that's got 60 million in P&L

themes.theme: Regimes, data relevance, and execution sensitivity

insights.claim: Strategies whose results degrade sharply with small execution delays (e.g. losing 20% of P&L from a 15-minute delay) carry bigger capacity concerns and less margin of error in forward application than timing-insensitive ones.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Prefer execution-insensitive systems for robustness and scale.
insights.quote: If you have one that if you delay by 15 minutes, you lose 20% of your P&L, you have one that's pretty time-sensitive

insights.claim: Early quants mistakenly model markets as a two-body problem where data moves prices; in reality data surprises don't buy or sell anything, people do, so data sensitivities vary across time.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Fixed data-to-price sensitivities are unstable; model participant behavior.
insights.quote: data changes and surprises don't buy or sell anything. People see those signals

insights.claim: Regimes also define which information matters: M1/M2/M3 money supply once led the Wall Street Journal front page but is now muted to the point a bright new hire would never think of it.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Monitor shifting market focus on data, not fixed indicators.
insights.quote: the M1, M2 and M3 money supply used to be on the front page of the Wall Street Journal

insights.claim: Regime identification is imperfect but works as a setup: one should trade differently in a high-inflation, rising-rate, supply-constrained world than in a demand-constrained, low-rate, low-inflation world.
insights.speaker: Pat Welton
insights.so_what: Regime conditioning belongs in the setup step, not as precise prediction.
insights.quote: you might want to trade differently in a high inflation, you know, rising interest rate, supply constrained world
